name: Heterogeneous Perception of Safety: Santiago Street Pairs
description:
Method replication: same task, answer options and design as the paper; the images are not the paper's stimuli (new Google Street View views of Santiago, © Google). Ramírez, Hurtubia, Lobel & Rossetti (2021, Landscape and Urban Planning 208:104002) ran a perception survey of public spaces that first collected respondents' sociodemographics and then asked them to compare pairs of street images, and fitted a discrete choice model whose image attributes came from semantic segmentation and object detection. Safety perception differed by gender and by the observer's habitual travel mode; the model was then applied to map safety perception across Santiago, Chile, for different types of users.

What participants do: after consent, they give gender, age, nationality, country of residence, education and main transport mode. Then they compare pairs of Santiago street views: 15 pairs on "Which place looks safer?" and 5 pairs each on more walkable, more livable, more beautiful and wealthier, always with an explicit "equally" answer. Pairs are drawn at random from 70 images.

Analysis as in the paper: choice models (ordinal or binary logit with ties) of which image wins, with image attributes from segmentation and object counts, interacted with respondent gender and travel mode to test heterogeneous perception. The platform's pairwise scores (win rate, TrueSkill) give a first look.

Differences from the original study: (1) the images are 70 new Google Street View views (2016–2026) from random points in central Santiago, not the paper's image set; (2) the original let respondents continue with unlimited pairs; this template asks 15 safety pairs and 5 pairs for each other perception. The earlier version of this template showed 4 photographs cropped from the paper PDF.
